name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_DIA_Q01 - Refraction of a plane wavefront through a thin prism

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates a plane light wave incident horizontally from the left on a glass prism of refractive index \(n > 1\):

Which of the following physical statements correctly explains why the emerging wavefront is tilted as shown?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic diagram depicts a plane wavefront propagating in air and striking a glass prism whose base is wider than its apex. The refractive index of the glass is \(n > 1\), and the speed of light in vacuum/air is \(c\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Physical Principles
According to wave theory, a wavefront is a surface of constant phase. When a wavefront passes from air into a medium of refractive index \(n\), the speed of propagation decreases from \(c\) to: \[ v = \frac{c}{n} \] The frequency of light \(\nu\) remains unchanged across the interface.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Optical Path
The time \(\Delta t\) taken by light to travel a geometric thickness \(d\) inside a medium of refractive index \(n\) is: \[ \Delta t = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{n d}{c} \] Because \(v < c\), traversing a greater thickness of glass requires a longer transit time (suffering a larger phase retardation or delay).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Analysis of the Wavefront
In the triangular prism geometry shown in the figure: 1. Near the top (apex), the thickness of the glass traversed by the upper portion of the wavefront is very small (\(d_{\text{top}} \to 0\)), so it spends most of its time traveling at the faster speed \(c\) in air. 2. Near the bottom (base), the thickness of the glass traversed by the lower portion of the wavefront is greatest (\(d_{\text{bottom}} = d_{\text{max}}\)), so it travels at the slower speed \(v = c/n\) over a significant distance. 3. As a result, the lower portion of the wavefront is delayed the most relative to the upper portion. 4. When emerging into air, the lag in the lower section tilts the plane of constant phase backward at the bottom, resulting in an emerging plane wavefront tilted toward the base of the prism.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The physical cause of the tilt is that the lower section of the wavefront traverses the thickest portion of the slower medium and experiences the greatest delay. Thus, the statement attributing the tilt to the greater time delay suffered by the lower portion traversing a greater thickness of slower medium is correct.

answer.text: The lower portion of the wavefront traverses a greater thickness of glass where light propagates more slowly, causing it to suffer a greater time delay than the upper portion.
The upper portion of the wavefront travels through a greater thickness of glass, causing it to lag behind the lower portion.
The speed of light increases inside the glass prism, causing the lower portion of the wavefront to advance ahead of the upper portion.
The frequency of light decreases inside the glass prism, resulting in an angular deflection of the wavefront without any differential time delay.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_DIA_Q02 - Geometry and curvature of wavefront emerging from a convex lens

questiontext.text:
A plane monochromatic light wave is incident normally on a thin convex lens of focal length \(f\), as shown in the diagram below:

What is the geometric shape and radius of curvature of the emerging wavefront?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram illustrates a parallel beam of light (plane wavefront) incident parallel to the principal axis on a converging convex lens having focal length \(f\). The emerging wavefront is shown converging toward the focus \(F\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Physical Principles
1. Light rays are the orthogonal trajectories (normals) to the wavefronts. 2. The speed of light is lower in the glass lens than in air. 3. According to Fermat's principle and wave optics, the total optical transit time between corresponding points on an incident wavefront and the conjugate image point is identical along every ray path.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Geometric Construction
A thin convex lens is thickest at the optical center and thinnest at the periphery. - The central ray traverses the maximum thickness of glass and is delayed the most. - Marginal rays travel mostly through air with minimal glass thickness and experience the least delay. Consequently, upon exiting the lens, the central part of the wavefront lags behind the peripheral edges, producing a central depression (concavity facing the direction of propagation).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Characterization of the Wavefront
1. Since all refracted rays converge toward the focal point \(F\) located at distance \(f\) along the principal axis, the orthogonal surface to these converging rays must be spherical. 2. The center of curvature of this spherical surface is the focal point \(F\). 3. Immediately upon emergence, the distance from any point on this wavefront to the focal point \(F\) equals the focal length \(f\). 4. Therefore, the emerging wavefront is a converging spherical wavefront with radius of curvature equal to \(f\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The emerging wavefront is spherical, converging, and centered at the focal point \(F\), possessing a radius of curvature \(R = f\). Hence, the correct conceptual answer corresponds to a spherical wavefront converging toward the focal point with radius of curvature equal to the focal length.

answer.text: Cylindrical wavefront diverging outward with a radius of curvature equal to \(2f\)
Spherical wavefront converging toward the focal point \(F\) with a radius of curvature equal to \(f\)
Spherical wavefront diverging away from the lens center with a radius of curvature equal to \(f/2\)
Plane wavefront propagating along the optical axis with infinite radius of curvature

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_DIA_Q03 - Refractive index calculation from Huygens construction geometry

questiontext.text:
The figure below shows Huygens' geometrical construction for a plane wavefront \(AB\) undergoing refraction at the planar boundary separating Medium 1 and Medium 2:

In time \(\tau\), the incident wavefront advances a distance \(BC = v_1 \tau = 6.0\text{ cm}\) in Medium 1, while the secondary wavelet in Medium 2 expands to a radius \(AE = v_2 \tau = 4.0\text{ cm}\). What is the refractive index of Medium 2 with respect to Medium 1 (\(^{1}n_2\)), and does the ray bend towards or away from the normal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the geometric layout: - Distance advanced by the incident wavefront in Medium 1 during time \(\tau\): \(BC = v_1 \tau = 6.0\text{ cm}\). - Radius of the secondary wavelet in Medium 2 during the identical time interval \(\tau\): \(AE = v_2 \tau = 4.0\text{ cm}\). - The common hypotenuse shared by the two right-angled triangles \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle AEC\) along the interface is \(AC\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
1. Both media are homogeneous and isotropic. 2. The angle of incidence \(i = \angle BAC\) satisfies \(\sin i = \frac{BC}{AC}\). 3. The angle of refraction \(r = \angle ECA\) satisfies \(\sin r = \frac{AE}{AC}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Snell's law derived from Huygens' construction: \[ \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{BC / AC}{AE / AC} = \frac{v_1 \tau}{v_2 \tau} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} \] The refractive index of Medium 2 relative to Medium 1 is defined as: \[ ^{1}n_2 = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substituting the given lengths into the ratio: \[ ^{1}n_2 = \frac{BC}{AE} = \frac{6.0\text{ cm}}{4.0\text{ cm}} = 1.50 \] Since \(v_2 < v_1\) (\(4.0\text{ cm} < 6.0\text{ cm}\)), Medium 2 is optically denser than Medium 1. Consequently: \[ \sin r < \sin i \implies r < i \] The angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence, meaning the refracted ray bends towards the normal.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ratio \(6.0/4.0 = 1.50\) gives a relative refractive index greater than unity, confirming that light slows down in Medium 2 and refracts toward the normal line. Therefore, the refractive index is \(1.50\) and the ray bends towards the normal.

answer.text: \(^{1}n_2 = 0.67\), and the refracted ray bends away from the normal
\(^{1}n_2 = 1.33\), and the refracted ray bends away from the normal
\(^{1}n_2 = 1.50\), and the refracted ray bends towards the normal
\(^{1}n_2 = 2.25\), and the refracted ray bends towards the normal

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_DIA_Q04 - Path difference and fringe order determination in YDSE

questiontext.text:
In the Young's double-slit arrangement shown below, monochromatic light of wavelength \(\lambda = 500\text{ nm}\) is used:

The slits \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are separated by \(d = 0.20\text{ mm}\), and the viewing screen is placed at a distance \(D = 1.0\text{ m}\). What is the optical path difference \(\Delta x = S_2P - S_1P\) at point \(P\) located at distance \(x = 7.5\text{ mm}\) from the central maximum \(O\), and what type of fringe is formed at \(P\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the schematic diagram and problem statement: - Slit separation: \(d = 0.20\text{ mm} = 0.20 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\) - Distance to screen: \(D = 1.0\text{ m}\) - Position of point \(P\) from center \(O\): \(x = 7.5\text{ mm} = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\) - Wavelength of light: \(\lambda = 500\text{ nm} = 500 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Approximations
Since \(d \ll D\) (\(0.20\text{ mm} \ll 1.0\text{ m}\)) and \(x \ll D\) (\(7.5\text{ mm} \ll 1.0\text{ m}\)), the paraxial approximation holds valid, meaning \(\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta \approx \frac{x}{D}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
1. The optical path difference between the waves arriving at point \(P\) is: \[ \Delta x = S_2P - S_1P \approx \frac{x d}{D} \] 2. Condition for bright fringe (constructive interference): \[ \Delta x = n\lambda \quad (n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots) \] 3. Condition for dark fringe (destructive interference): \[ \Delta x = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda \quad (n = 0, 1, 2, \dots) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the given values to find the path difference: \[ \Delta x = \frac{(7.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m})(0.20 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m})}{1.0\text{ m}} = 1.50 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m} = 1500\text{ nm} \] Now, compare \(\Delta x\) with the wavelength \(\lambda\): \[ n = \frac{\Delta x}{\lambda} = \frac{1500\text{ nm}}{500\text{ nm}} = 3 \] Since \(n = 3\) is an exact integer, constructive interference takes place at point \(P\), forming the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) bright fringe.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The fringe width is \(\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d} = \frac{500 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.0}{0.20 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.5\text{ mm}\). The position of the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) bright fringe is \(x_3 = 3\beta = 3 \times 2.5\text{ mm} = 7.5\text{ mm}\), which perfectly matches the given coordinate. Thus, the path difference is \(1500\text{ nm}\), forming the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) bright fringe.

answer.text: \(\Delta x = 500\text{ nm}\), forming the \(1^{\text{st}}\) bright fringe
\(\Delta x = 1000\text{ nm}\), forming the \(2^{\text{nd}}\) bright fringe
\(\Delta x = 1250\text{ nm}\), forming the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) dark fringe
\(\Delta x = 1500\text{ nm}\), forming the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) bright fringe

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_DIA_Q05 - Intensity ratio of first secondary maximum to central maximum in diffraction

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the intensity distribution \(I(\theta)\) as a function of the diffraction angle \(\theta\) for Fraunhofer diffraction through a single slit of width \(a\):

The central diffraction maximum has peak intensity \(I_0\). Using the wave theory of diffraction where the first secondary maximum occurs at approximately \(\theta \approx \frac{3\lambda}{2a}\), what is the ratio of the intensity of the first secondary maximum \(I_1\) to the central maximum intensity \(I_0\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph represents single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction: - Slit width: \(a\) - Monochromatic wavelength: \(\lambda\) - Central peak intensity at \(\theta = 0\): \(I_0\) - Position of first secondary maximum: \(\theta \approx \frac{3\lambda}{2a} = 1.5\frac{\lambda}{a}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Physical Model
The slit is treated as a continuous distribution of Huygens secondary wavelet sources oscillating in phase. The resultant amplitude and intensity are obtained by integrating across the slit aperture.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
The intensity distribution for single-slit diffraction is given by: \[ I(\theta) = I_0 \left(\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\right)^2 \] where the phase parameter \(\beta\) is defined as: \[ \beta = \frac{\pi a \sin\theta}{\lambda} \approx \frac{\pi a \theta}{\lambda} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Evaluation of the Intensity Ratio
1. For the first secondary maximum, substituting \(\theta \approx \frac{3\lambda}{2a}\) into the expression for \(\beta\): \[ \beta \approx \frac{\pi a}{\lambda} \left(\frac{3\lambda}{2a}\right) = \frac{3\pi}{2} \] 2. Evaluating \(\sin\beta\) at \(\beta = \frac{3\pi}{2}\): \[ \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1 \implies \sin^2\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 1 \] 3. Substituting this into the intensity expression: \[ I_1 = I_0 \left(\frac{\sin(3\pi/2)}{3\pi/2}\right)^2 = I_0 \left(\frac{-1}{3\pi/2}\right)^2 = I_0 \left(\frac{2}{3\pi}\right)^2 = I_0 \left(\frac{4}{9\pi^2}\right) \] 4. Computing the numerical fraction: \[ \frac{I_1}{I_0} = \frac{4}{9\pi^2} \approx \frac{4}{9 \times 9.8696} = \frac{4}{88.826} \approx 0.045 \quad (4.5\%) \]

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Only about one-third of the slit sends secondary wavelets that remain uncancelled at the first secondary maximum, giving an amplitude of approximately \(A_0 / (1.5\pi)\), which squares to \(\frac{4}{9\pi^2} \approx 4.5\%\) of the central intensity. Therefore, the ratio \(\frac{I_1}{I_0}\) is \(\frac{4}{9\pi^2} \approx 0.045\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WAVE_OPTICS_DIA_Q06 - Transmitted intensity through two polaroids using Malus law

questiontext.text:
An unpolarized beam of light with an incident intensity of \(I_{\text{in}} = 80\text{ W/m}^2\) passes through two ideal polaroids, \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), as shown in the schematic diagram below:

The first polaroid \(P_1\) has its transmission axis oriented vertically. The second polaroid \(P_2\) (analyzer) has its transmission axis tilted at an angle \(\theta = 60^\circ\) relative to the vertical transmission axis of \(P_1\). What is the intensity of the light emerging from \(P_2\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the schematic layout: - Incident light: Unpolarized light of intensity \(I_{\text{in}} = 80\text{ W/m}^2\) - Polarizer \(P_1\): Pass-axis aligned vertically - Analyzer \(P_2\): Pass-axis tilted at an angle \(\theta = 60^\circ\) with respect to the pass-axis of \(P_1\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Physical Principles
1. Both polaroids are ideal (transmitting \(100\%\) of the electric field component parallel to their respective pass-axes and absorbing \(100\%\) of the perpendicular component). 2. Unpolarized light consists of equal time-averaged intensity contributions in all transverse vibration directions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
1. Passage of unpolarized light through a single ideal polarizer halves its intensity: \[ I_1 = \frac{I_{\text{in}}}{2} \] 2. According to Malus's law, when linearly polarized light of intensity \(I_1\) passes through an analyzer whose axis is oriented at an angle \(\theta\) relative to the plane of polarization, the transmitted intensity is: \[ I_2 = I_1 \cos^2\theta \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Calculation
1. Intensity after passing through \(P_1\): \[ I_1 = \frac{80\text{ W/m}^2}{2} = 40\text{ W/m}^2 \] The light emerging from \(P_1\) is completely linearly polarized along the vertical axis. 2. The angle between the transmission axes of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) is \(\theta = 60^\circ\). 3. Applying Malus's law for the transmission through \(P_2\): \[ I_2 = I_1 \cos^2(60^\circ) \] Since \(\cos(60^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}\): \[ \cos^2(60^\circ) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \] 4. Calculating the final transmitted intensity: \[ I_2 = 40\text{ W/m}^2 \times \frac{1}{4} = 10\text{ W/m}^2 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\text{W/m}^2\), and the numerical value is physically consistent: \(80 \to 40 \to 10\text{ W/m}^2\). Thus, the transmitted intensity emerging from the second polaroid is \(10\text{ W/m}^2\).
